It's a control application that runs on a tablet and sets the infusion rate on our
own infusion pump. The pump is a Class III device. The app doesn't diagnose anything
— it just lets the clinician set and adjust the rate, and it shows the current rate.
Intended purpose: "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under

# MDR Software Classification: infusion pump control app

**Intended purpose (as stated):** "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control."
**Qualified as a device:** assumed established — you're treating it as in scope; Art. 2(1) qualification is outside what I verify here.

## Class: III

**Route:** 3.3 → drives a device → same class as the driven device (the Class III pump). Rule 11 is never reached.

## Reasoning

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Intended purpose | "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control" | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Drives or influences another device? | **Yes** — setting and adjusting the delivery rate is driving the pump, not merely displaying its output | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Consequence | Falls within the same class as that device → **III** | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Which limb | **Not reached** — Rule 11 only applies to software independent of any other device | `[verified]` |
| 3.5 | Could a stricter rule apply? | No — III is the top class; nothing can go higher | `[verified]` |

The "it doesn't diagnose anything" point is the thing to set aside. That framing is a Rule 11 argument, and Rule 11 is only for software that is *independent of any other device*. Under 3.3 your app isn't independent — it takes the pump's class whatever Rule 11 would have said on its own. Same for "it just shows the current rate": display alone would suggest independence, but the app doesn't just display. Setting the delivery rate is the driving function, and one driving function is enough.

"Under clinician control" doesn't change this either. 3.3 has no carve-out for a human in the loop; the software still sets the parameter the pump acts on.

## What would change this

- **The app stops setting the rate.** If the intended purpose were narrowed to display only — read the current rate, no writes to the pump — 3.3 would likely not bite and it would be classified in its own right under Rule 11. That is a real product change, not a documentation change.
- **The pump's own class is wrong.** Your class is derived from the pump's, so it moves if the pump's does. Worth confirming the Class III call on the pump is settled (it isn't a Rule 11 question and I don't carry the rules that decide it — `[verify]`, likely Rule 12 on administration of medicinal products).
- **A second, separable software product.** If display and control are genuinely distinct devices with distinct intended purposes, 3.2 applies the rules separately to each. Splitting them to get a lower class on the viewer only works if they really are separate devices with separate purposes and documentation — not one app described two ways.

## Limits

> This classifies software under MDR Annex VIII implementing rules 3.1–3.7 and Rule 11, retrieved verbatim from EUR-Lex on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover Art. 2(1) qualification, Rules 1–10 or 12–22, Annex XVI, IVDR, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, or national interpretation. Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

This is the Annex VIII text applied to the intended purpose as you stated it. The class drives your conformity route, whether you need a notified body, and the depth of your technical documentation, so confirm it with your regulatory lead or notified body before building on it. The three things to put in front of them:

1. **The 3.3 call** — that setting the delivery rate is "driving" the pump, so the app inherits its class rather than being classified in its own right.
2. **That Rule 11 is not reached at all** — the no-diagnosis argument doesn't apply, because Rule 11 only reaches independent software.
3. **The pump's Class III determination** — your class is entirely derived from it, so it needs to be solid.

Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

## Short answer: Class III

Your app inherits the pump's class. That comes from MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, **implementing rule 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Setting and adjusting the delivery rate is the textbook case of *driving* a device — it's not merely "influencing" it. So the pump is Class III → the app is Class III.

## Why "it doesn't diagnose" doesn't get you to Class I

That reasoning is a Rule 11 argument, and **Rule 11 doesn't apply here**. Rule 11 governs software that is independent of another device — MDSW that provides information for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions, or monitors physiological processes. Per MDCG 2019-11, driving/influencing software is classified under rule 3.3 instead, and you never reach Rule 11's "all other software is Class I" catch-all.

Two related traps in your framing:

- **"Under clinician control" is not a de-risking factor.** A human in the loop doesn't lower the class when the software is the thing that actually commands the delivery rate. If the app sends a wrong rate, or the displayed rate diverges from the delivered rate, the clinician's oversight is exactly what's been defeated.
- **"It just shows the current rate" is a safety-relevant function**, not a passive one. Displaying delivery rate is part of the control loop, and rule 3.3 covers it regardless.

## The prior question you should settle first

Is the app a **separate device** or a **component of the pump**? You said it's your own pump, which makes this live:

- **Component / part of the pump system** — same manufacturer, placed on the market as part of the pump with a single intended purpose and a single technical file. Then it isn't classified separately at all; it's covered by the pump's Class III certificate, and your job is to get it into that device's design controls, risk management, and NB scope.
- **Separate device in its own right** — placed on the market independently (e.g. app-store distribution, sold or CE-marked separately, own intended-purpose statement). Then it's its own Class III device with its own certificate, UDI, declaration of conformity, and clinical evaluation.

The fact that you have a standalone intended purpose statement written for it suggests you may be heading toward the second, which is materially more expensive. If it's genuinely inseparable from the pump, the first route is usually the right one — but that's a decision to make deliberately, not by drift.

## One thing worth verifying

Infusion pumps are commonly **Class IIb** under MDR (Rule 12, devices for administering medicinal products; escalated to III typically for implanted pumps, drug-device combinations, or closed-loop delivery of hazardous substances). Since the app's class is a direct copy of the pump's, confirm the pump's Class III basis is correct and documented — if the pump is actually IIb, so is the app.

## What Class III means downstream

- Annex IX conformity assessment: full QMS + technical documentation assessment by your notified body, **including design dossier examination** (Annex IX Chapter II) — not a route where the app can ride along unexamined.
- **IEC 62304 software safety Class C** — the app can contribute to death or serious injury via over-infusion, and there's no plausible external risk-control measure that segregates it down to B.
- Clinical evaluation under Article 61 with the higher Class III expectations, plus PMCF.
- IEC 62366-1 usability engineering is central here — rate-entry UI is where the real hazards live (decimal misplacement, unit confusion, unconfirmed changes).
- Because it's on a **general-purpose tablet**: you own the computing-platform requirements — OS version control, what happens on app crash / backgrounding / low battery / lost connectivity, and MDCG 2019-16 cybersecurity. A "fail safe" story for the pump when the controller disappears is mandatory.

Worth confirming the component-vs-separate-device call with your notified body before you build the technical file around either assumption — that choice is harder to reverse than the classification itself, and this analysis is engineering guidance, not a regulatory sign-off.

**Class III** — the app inherits the pump's class.

## Why

MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, **implementing rule 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Your app sets and adjusts the delivery rate. That is driving the device in the most direct sense — it is the control path for therapy delivery. So it takes the pump's class: III.

## The rule you should *not* use

Regulatory folks often reach for **Rule 11** here and land on IIa. That's the wrong rule. Rule 11 applies to MDSW that *provides information* used for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions, or that monitors physiological processes. Per **MDCG 2019-11**, software that drives or influences the use of a hardware device is not MDSW in its own right — it's classified with the device, i.e. rule 3.3. And even if you argued Rule 11 also applied (the "shows the current rate" display), implementing rule **3.5** says the highest applicable class wins. Still III.

The fact that the app doesn't diagnose is irrelevant to classification — control of therapy is enough.

## Two things to pin down

**1. Is the app a separate device, or part of the pump?** Both end in Class III rigor, but the routing differs:
- *Part of the pump system* (one CE certificate, one tech file, shipped as the pump's UI) — most likely given it's your own pump. No separate classification; it's a software component of the Class III device, covered by the pump's technical documentation, and rate-setting becomes part of the pump's V&V and risk file.
- *Placed on the market separately* (own CE mark, own UDI-DI, own technical documentation, own Annex IX assessment) — then rule 3.3 classifies it Class III in its own right.

**2. Verify *why* the pump is Class III**, because you inherit that. Class III isn't the default for infusion pumps — Rule 12 caps administering medicinal products in a potentially hazardous manner at **IIb**. Class III usually comes from Rule 14 (incorporates an ancillary medicinal substance) or **Rule 22** (active therapeutic device with integrated diagnostic function that significantly determines patient management — closed-loop). If the pump is actually IIb, your app is IIb. If it's III via Rule 22 and your app participates in the titration/closed loop, that reinforces III.

## What this means in practice

- Notified Body conformity assessment under **Annex IX** (QMS + per-product technical documentation assessment for Class III), or Annex X+XI.
- **IEC 62304 safety class C** almost certainly — a wrong rate is a plausible death/serious-injury path. Note 62304 class is independent of MDR class, but here they align.
- Clinical investigation generally expected (Art. 61(4)), unless you can leverage the pump family's existing data.
- **SSCP** (Art. 32), annual **PSUR** (Art. 86), PMCF plan. Article 54 CECP does *not* apply — that's Class III *implantable* and Class IIb active administering devices.

The thing I'd worry about most: a consumer tablet and a wireless link are now a safety-critical control path. Expect hard NB questions on loss-of-link behaviour (the pump must hold last commanded rate and never act on a partial command), OS-as-SOUP and OS updates, minimum platform specification, touch mis-entry and IEC 62366-1 usability for rate entry, and whether any **alarms** are annunciated on the app — reviewers are generally unwilling to see safety alarms depend on general-purpose hardware, so those usually have to stay on the pump. Relevant: IEC 62366-1, IEC 60601-2-24, IEC 60601-1-8, IEC 81001-5-1, IEC 60601-1-2 plus AAMI TIR69 for the wireless link.

This is my reading of the rules, not regulatory advice — confirm the final classification and the separate-device-vs-component question with your Notified Body, since it drives your whole submission strategy.

Memory directory isn't readable in this session, so I can't check or save notes there — here's the answer.

## Class III

Not IIa, not IIb. The reasoning most people get wrong here is that they reach for Rule 11 (the "software rule") and land on IIa. Rule 11 doesn't apply to your app.

**The rule that governs is an implementing rule, not a classification rule.** MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, §3.3:

> *Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right.*

Your app sets the delivery rate. That is the textbook definition of "drives a device." So it inherits the pump's class — III. You never get to the Annex VIII Chapter III rules at all.

**Why Rule 11 is a red herring:** Rule 11 covers software *intended to provide information which is used to take decisions*. It's about software that outputs information to a human who then acts. Yours acts on the pump directly. MDCG 2019-11 draws exactly this line — "software driving or influencing the use of a device" is a separate category from MDSW subject to Rule 11.

Two things in your framing that feel like they should lower the class but don't:

- **"It doesn't diagnose anything."** Irrelevant. Diagnosis is one route into Rule 11; therapy delivery is the other, and driving-software bypasses both.
- **"Under clinician control."** Also irrelevant. A clinician is in the loop on essentially every infusion pump, and the hazard — an entered or transmitted rate that isn't the intended rate — is not mitigated by the clinician being the one who typed it. If anything, the human-in-the-loop is the *source* of the classic overinfusion hazard (decimal point, wrong units, wrong concentration), which is why IEC 62366-1 usability engineering will be a focal point of your NB review.

The "shows the current rate" function is a monitoring/display claim that on its own might sit lower, but classification takes the highest applicable class across all the intended purposes, so it doesn't move anything.

## Two things to verify before you bank on this

**1. Is the pump genuinely Class III?** This matters because your app's class is entirely derivative. Under MDR Rule 12, a typical external infusion pump lands in **IIb** ("administering medicinal products... in a manner that is potentially hazardous"). Class III for a pump usually means one of: it's active *implantable* (Rule 8), it incorporates a medicinal substance (Rule 14), or it's indicated for a therapy that pulls it up. If someone carried "Class III" over from an old MDD determination or an FDA classification (FDA Class II/III uses a completely different scheme and doesn't map), re-derive it. If the pump turns out to be IIb, your app is IIb.

**2. Is the app a *part* of the pump, or a device placed on the market in its own right?** Same manufacturer, so you have a genuine choice, and it's the bigger commercial decision:

- **As a component of the pump system** — it lives inside the pump's technical documentation, shares its CE certificate, its UDI-DI, its declaration of conformity. One certificate to maintain. But every app release is a change to a Class III device, so it runs through your change-control and possibly notified body notification for significant changes. Ties your app release cadence to pump lifecycle governance.
- **As a standalone device / accessory** — its own classification (still III via §3.3), own UDI, own DoC, own clinical evaluation and PMCF. More overhead, but decouples release cycles and lets you support multiple pump models.

For a single-pump control app from the pump's own manufacturer, folding it into the pump's technical documentation is usually the cleaner path. If you're planning to support a family of pumps or third-party ones later, standalone is worth the overhead.

## What Class III actually costs you

- **Conformity assessment**: Annex IX (full QMS + technical documentation assessment, including design examination) or Annex X+XI. No self-certification, no Annex IX Chapter I-only shortcut.
- **Clinical evaluation** under Article 61, with a **PMCF plan mandatory** and a **PSUR annually** (not every two years).
- **IEC 62304 software safety class C** almost certainly — overinfusion can contribute to death. Note this is a *separate* determination from the MDR class; you can't infer one from the other, though here they both come out at the top. Class C means full architectural design, detailed design down to unit level, and unit verification documented.
- **Standards in scope**: IEC 62304, IEC 62366-1 (usability — do a proper summative validation on rate entry), ISO 14971, IEC 82304-1 (health software products), and IEC 60601-1 / 60601-1-8 / **60601-2-24** apply at the pump-plus-app system level even though your part is software. Plus MDCG 2019-16 for cybersecurity.
- **The tablet is uncontrolled hardware.** Your risk file needs to handle OS auto-updates, competing apps, touchscreen mis-registration, display failure or dimming, battery depletion mid-infusion, and loss of the pump link. Specify minimum hardware/OS in the IFU and state what happens to a running infusion when the app dies — the pump must fail safe independently.

One drafting note: your intended purpose statement is thin for a Class III submission. Expect the notified body to want patient population, clinical setting, user profile, the drug classes/therapies in scope, and explicit exclusions. That sentence is also what fixes your classification, so it's worth writing precisely before it's load-bearing.

Standard caveat: this is the analysis, not a determination — your RA function owns the written classification rationale and your notified body has the final say. But I'd be surprised if either landed anywhere other than "same class as the pump."

## Short answer: **Class III** under Rule 11, on the intended purpose as written.

## 1. Qualification

It's a medical device in its own right, not an accessory. Article 2(1) covers software intended for "diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis" — flagging suspected LVO is diagnostic. Under MDCG 2019-11 it's MDSW because it performs an action on data beyond storage/archival/communication/simple search, and it does so for the benefit of an individual patient.

Your "no connection to any other device" point is handled explicitly by Annex VIII, implementing rule **3.3**: software that drives or influences another device takes that device's class; *"if the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."* So standalone status doesn't lower anything — it just means you classify the software on its own merits, which is what Rule 11 does.

## 2. Rule 11, first limb

> Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is class IIa, **except** if such decisions have an impact that may cause:
> — death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health → **class III**
> — a serious deterioration of a person's state of health or a surgical intervention → **class IIb**

Two steps:

**Does it provide information used to take a diagnostic/therapeutic decision?** Yes — your intended purpose says so in terms: "to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy." That's the trigger phrase for the rule, essentially verbatim.

**What's the impact of a wrong decision?** A false negative means an LVO patient is not taken to thrombectomy inside the treatment window. The expected consequence is death or permanent neurological deficit — the first indent, not the second. A false positive is also bad (an unnecessary endovascular procedure, which is at minimum the "surgical intervention" indent and carries its own mortality), but classification takes the worst credible outcome and Rule 3.5 says the highest applicable class wins.

That lands on **Class III**.

## 3. The argument for IIb, and why I don't think it holds here

The usual route to IIb is to argue the software isn't *significant* to the decision — the neurointerventionalist independently reviews the CTA anyway, the tool only reorders a worklist, so the software can't itself cause the missed treatment. Worth knowing two things about that:

- MDR has **no clinician-in-the-loop carve-out**. That's a US concept (21st Century Cures §520(o), FDA's CDS guidance). MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that a human making the final call does not reduce the class. Under MDR the question is what the information is *for* and how bad it is if wrong.
- Your own intended purpose forecloses it. "Support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy" is driving clinical management, not administrative prioritisation.

If you genuinely want to argue a lower class, that has to be a **product and labelling decision made now**, not a classification argument made later: no diagnostic claim, output framed as notification/workflow prioritisation only, explicit statement that it does not replace image review and is not to be used to decide treatment, no LVO "flag" presented as a finding. That's a materially different product, it's still likely IIa at best, and notified bodies have been sceptical of the reframing where the clinical workflow clearly reacts to the output. My recommendation is to classify at III and design for it rather than build a IIb dossier you may have to redo.

## 4. What Class III commits you to

- Notified body **Annex IX** conformity assessment: full QMS audit **plus** technical documentation assessment of *this device* (not sampling, as at IIa).
- Annex IX Section 5.1 **clinical evaluation consultation procedure** — the expert panel referral. Budget real calendar time.
- **Article 61(4)**: clinical investigations are expected for implantable and Class III devices. You're not implantable, so the derogation route via equivalence or existing data is open in principle, but for a novel algorithm you should plan on your own prospective clinical data — standalone sensitivity/specificity against a neuroradiology reference standard, ideally with clinical-workflow endpoints (door-to-groin time).
- **PSUR updated annually** and submitted to the NB (Art. 86), PMCF plan, SSCP required, UDI/EUDAMED, Class III implant card N/A.
- Downstream: **IEC 62304 software safety class C**, IEC 14971, IEC 82304-1, and for the ML component expect the NB to press hard on training/test data provenance, demographic and scanner-vendor generalisation, off-distribution behaviour, and change control for retraining. Also GSPR 17 (Annex I) and, once applicable, the AI Act — an MDR Class III device with an NB is **high-risk** under Annex I of the AI Act, so plan the two conformity assessments together.

## One drafting note

"Provide triage information" and "support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy" pull in different directions in the same sentence — the first sounds like workflow, the second is unambiguously therapeutic decision support. Pick one and be consistent across the IFU, the technical documentation, the clinical evaluation and your marketing material. Inconsistency there is a reliable way to attract NB findings, and marketing claims that outrun the IFU are a common source of them.

## 2. Classification under Rule 11

Rule 11, first paragraph, is a three-step ladder:

| Impact of the decision the information informs | Class |
|---|---|
| Baseline — information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes | IIa |
| Serious deterioration of health, or a surgical intervention | IIb |
| **Death or irreversible deterioration of health** | **III** |

**Step 1 — does the baseline bite?** Yes. Your stated intended purpose is explicit that the output is used "to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy." That is information used to take a decision with a therapeutic purpose. You are at least IIa; there's no arguing this into the "information used for non-decision purposes" bucket.

**Step 2 — escalate.** Assess the impact of an *erroneous* output on both sides:

- **False negative** (LVO missed / not flagged): thrombectomy delayed or not performed within the treatment window. The clinical consequence is a completed large-territory infarct — permanent hemiplegia, aphasia, dependency, or death. That is squarely "death or an irreversible deterioration."
- **False positive**: patient taken for an unnecessary intra-arterial procedure — vessel dissection, intracranial haemorrhage, periprocedural stroke, death. Also in the top tier.

Either failure mode alone lands you in **Class III**.

**Step 3 — is the human in the loop a mitigation?** No, not for classification purposes. Classification under Annex VIII is driven by intended purpose and the potential harm of the information provided; it is not reduced by the assumption that the neurointerventionalist would catch the error, and it is not reduced by risk-control measures you implement. Risk controls belong in your ISO 14971 file, not in the Rule 11 analysis. Reviewers are consistently strict on this point.

Rule 11's second and third paragraphs (monitoring of vital physiological parameters) don't apply. Rule 22 (active therapeutic with integrated diagnostic function determining patient management) doesn't apply either — no closed loop, no therapeutic delivery. If it did, it would also be III, so implementing rule 3.5 (highest class wins) changes nothing.

The intended purpose as written is what makes this Class III rather than IIb. Some LVO tools on the market are positioned as pure **notification/prioritisation** software: intended purpose limited to alerting a specialist to review images sooner, with an explicit statement that the output is not intended to be used for diagnosis or treatment decisions and that diagnosis rests on the clinician's own review of the source images. That framing is argued down to IIb, sometimes IIa.

You cannot have it both ways. If the labelling says "notification only" but the actual clinical workflow, your clinical evidence, and your marketing describe it as informing the go/no-go on thrombectomy, a notified body will reclassify you — and MDCG 2019-11 is clear that the stated intended purpose must be consistent with actual claims. - **Notified body** conformity assessment: Annex IX (QMS + technical documentation assessment of the device, mandatory for every Class III device), or Annex X + XI. No self-certification route.
- **Clinical investigation** presumptively required under Art. 61(4), unless you can rely on the narrow exemptions (equivalence to your own already-marketed device, or sufficient clinical data meeting common specifications). Plan for a prospective study.

MDCG 2019-11 says software is *not* a device if its action on data is limited to storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression. - **Argument it's in scope:** "trend the readings over weeks" implies aggregation and derivation of a trend that isn't in any single reading, and your intended purpose ties it explicitly to nephrology consultations — i.e. monitoring a diagnosed chronic disease in an identified patient. Notified bodies and competent authorities read that combination as MDSW.

The clause "for review during scheduled nephrology consultations" is what pulls you in. It names a clinical user, a clinical specialty, and a clinical use. A plain data-entry diary with no medical claim would stay out; yours makes one.

## Step 2: Classification (if MDSW)

Rule 11 has three limbs:

1. **Information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes → IIa.** The nephrologist looks at weight and BP trends to judge fluid status and titrate antihypertensives. That's information feeding a therapeutic decision. → **IIa**
2. **Monitoring physiological processes → IIa**, escalating to IIb only for vital physiological parameters where variation could cause *immediate danger*. Blood pressure is a vital physiological parameter, but weeks-long trending with no alarms and no acute use is not immediate danger. → **IIa, not IIb**
3. **All other software → Class I.**

You don't reach the IIb/III escalations: no alarms, no acute decisions, clinician-in-the-loop at a scheduled visit, so no plausible path to death or serious/irreversible deterioration from the software itself.

**Class I** is only reachable if you argue the software provides information but for neither diagnostic/therapeutic decisions nor monitoring — hard to sustain once your intended purpose says "for review during nephrology consultations." In practice Rule 11's Class I limb is very narrow, because software that does nothing diagnostic or monitoring-related usually isn't a device in the first place.

Note also: being standalone and unconnected to any device doesn't help you. Annex VIII §3.3 only puts software in the *same* class as a device when it drives or influences that device; independent software is classified in its own right. "No alarms" and "not for acute decisions" limit severity, which caps you at IIa — they don't exempt you.

MDCG 2019-11's decision test asks whether the software performs an action on data **beyond storage, archival, communication, or simple search**. The same guidance says altering the *representation* of data — including for display purposes — doesn't by itself count as such an action.

An app that takes numbers the patient typed in, stores them, and draws them on a time axis is doing exactly that and nothing more. It's an electronic version of the paper BP diary the nephrologist already asks for, and a paper diary isn't a device. No alarms, no acute use, no device connection (so no accessory analysis), no derived output the clinician couldn't get by reading the list of numbers.

Your intended-purpose wording — "record and trend … for review during scheduled consultations" — is drafted well for this. It claims no diagnosis, monitoring in the regulatory sense, or decision support.

## If it is MDSW, it's IIa

Rule 11's first limb catches software providing information used for decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes → **IIa** by default. Escalation to IIb/III requires serious deterioration / surgical intervention or death — your facts (weeks-long trend, no alarms, no acute decisions) rule those out. The second limb, monitoring physiological processes, is also IIa; it only reaches IIb for vital parameters where variation could cause immediate danger, which you've expressly excluded.

The "all other software is Class I" fallback is a trap here. Once you concede the app is MDSW, its whole purpose is feeding a clinical review — you'd be arguing it drives no decisions while marketing it as decision input. Notified bodies and BfArM in particular don't accept that. So: non-device, or IIa.

## What flips it to IIa

Any of these, individually:

- Trend lines, moving averages, rate-of-change, or any computed metric
- Target ranges, colour-coded readings, shaded "normal" bands
- Flags, notifications, or "your weight is up 2 kg this week" messaging
- Interpretive text, dry-weight estimates, or fluid-overload inference
- Marketing copy that says "monitor," "detect," "early warning," or "helps manage CKD"

The last one is the most common failure. Regulators read the website and app-store listing as evidence of intended purpose, and CKD weight gain is a well-known fluid-overload signal — claims in that direction will be read as a monitoring purpose regardless of what the technical file says.

Treat non-device status as a **deliberate design constraint**, not a conclusion you reached once. Write down the qualification rationale against the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps, freeze the feature set at raw values + plain plot, and put a change-control gate on anything from the list above. Also add "not intended for diagnosis, monitoring, or treatment decisions; not for acute or emergency use" to the app and its listing.

If the roadmap already includes any interpretation — and for a CKD product it usually does within a release or two — budget for IIa now: notified body, ISO 13485, IEC 62304, clinical evaluation. That transition is far cheaper planned than discovered.

## Short answer

**Class I** — under Annex VIII, Chapter III, **Rule 11, final indent** ("all other software is classified as class I").

## The reasoning chain

**Rule 11 is the governing rule.** Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3 says software independent of any other device is classified in its own right, so you don't inherit the class of the modality or the RIS/PACS it talks to. Rule 11 has four limbs:

| Limb | Applies? |
|---|---|
| Provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic/therapeutic purposes → IIa (IIb/III by harm severity) | **No** — see below |
| Monitors physiological processes → IIa / IIb | No |
| Intended to monitor vital physiological parameters where variation could cause immediate danger → IIb | No |
| **All other software → I** | **Yes** |

**Why the first limb doesn't bite.** The decision-relevant information is created entirely by the radiologist and is already fixed at signature. Your software contributes no new information, no derived value, no prioritisation, no interpretation, no flagging. It changes presentation and destination only. The referring GP is making decisions on the radiologist's information, not on anything the software provides. Under MDCG 2019-11's decomposition of Rule 11 ("significance of the information provided to the decision" × "situation/condition"), the software's own contribution to the decision is null — you can't score a severity band on information the device didn't generate. MDCG 2021-24 takes the same line for software confined to storage, archival, lossless communication and simple reformatting.

**So the pipeline is:** independent software → Rule 11 → no limb 1–3 → Class I. No other rule up-classifies it (Rule 13, the active-device catch-all, is displaced by the more specific Rule 11; implementing rule 3.5's "highest class applies" has nothing to bind to).

## The premise you've excluded is the weak point

You've stipulated qualification, so I'll take it as given — but note that the arguments that make this Class I are the *same* arguments MDCG 2019-11 uses to conclude that reformat-and-route software isn't MDSW at all (it neither creates nor modifies medical information; changing format for viewing purposes is expressly excluded). A notified body or competent authority reviewing this is more likely to challenge "is it a device" than "is it Class I." Practically, that's fine: the answer is Class I either way, and Class I self-declaration doesn't require you to litigate the point with a notified body.

## Four things that would change the answer

Check these against the actual build, because "reformats and routes" often hides one of them:

1. **Parsing that extracts and re-presents clinical content selectively** — e.g. pulling findings vs. impression into separate fields, truncating, summarising, or generating a header from body text. That's creating new information → Rule 11 first limb → **IIa at minimum**.
2. **Any prioritisation or routing based on content** — e.g. critical-findings detection to escalate delivery. Same result, and plausibly **IIb** given radiology's harm profile.
3. **Lossy transformation** — character-set mangling, unit conversion, dropping structured-report elements, image thumbnails that get read. If the output can differ clinically from the signed report, you're no longer a transport layer.
4. **Handling images alongside the report**, where the GP views them for diagnosis in your renderer.

If none apply, Class I holds. Document the argument explicitly in the technical file: state that the software is a transport/presentation layer, that clinical content is bit-identical from input to output, and ideally verify that with an automated content-integrity check in your V&V.

Not nothing — self-declared doesn't mean unregulated:

- Annexes II/III technical documentation, Annex IV EU declaration of conformity, self-affixed CE mark, no notified body (it's not Is/Ir/Im/Ir).
- ISO 13485 QMS (Art. 10(9)), IEC 62304 lifecycle, IEC 82304-1, ISO 14971.
- Clinical evaluation under Art. 61 / Annex XIV — for Class I this is normally literature- and state-of-the-art-based, no clinical investigation.
- Basic UDI-DI + UDI, EUDAMED registration, PRRC (Art. 15), PMS plan and PMS report (Art. 85 — report, not PSUR, at Class I).
- No transitional relief: MDR-only since 26 May 2021, since it wasn't up-classified out of self-certification.
- Cybersecurity per Annex I §17 and MDCG 2019-16 matters more than the class suggests, since you're moving identifiable clinical data between organisations.

# MDR Software Classification: habit tracker

**Intended purpose (as stated):** NOT SUPPLIED — I have a feature description ("log water intake, steps and sleep; weekly wellness score; encouragement messages"), not an intended purpose as written in technical documentation.
**Qualified as a device:** not established

## Class: cannot conclude

Classification presumes qualification. Before there's a class, the product has to be a medical device under Art. 2(1), and nothing you've told me settles that — it's a separate analysis that Annex VIII doesn't perform. On the face of it, an app with no medical claim that logs lifestyle inputs and returns encouragement sounds like it sits outside the device definition entirely. But "sounds like" isn't the call, and it isn't mine to make.

If your regulatory lead confirms it is *not* a device, there is no MDR class, and that's the end of it.

## The problem with the marketing ask

Putting an MDR class on the website is itself a claim of device status. "Class I under MDR" tells a reader this is a regulated medical device — which is the opposite of the "no medical claims" position you're describing, and it drags in CE marking, a technical file, a UDI, and Art. 10 manufacturer obligations to back it up. If you're not a device, the accurate website statement is that the product is not a medical device and makes no medical claims. That's the sentence marketing should be asking for.

## The real risk here is the copy, not the code

Implementing rule 3.1 anchors everything to intended purpose as you state it — and marketing copy is one of the places a stated purpose gets made. `[verified]` Two phrases to watch:

- **"wellness score"** — if it gets described as indicating health status, flagging problems, or telling users something is wrong, that's a step toward a medical purpose, and Rule 11's second limb (software intended to monitor physiological processes, base class **IIa**) becomes a live question rather than an academic one. `[verified]`
- **"sleep tracking"** — framed as sleep *quality* insight it's lifestyle; framed as detecting a sleep disorder it isn't.

The engineering doesn't change. The classification does. This is worth saying to marketing directly: the website copy can create the regulatory obligation that the product was built to avoid.

## What would change this

- A confirmed Art. 2(1) qualification determination, either way — this is the blocker.
- The intended purpose as written in your technical documentation, which I'd need to run 3.3 and Rule 11 properly.
- Whether the app takes data from, or feeds anything into, another device (a wearable, a connected scale). Under 3.3, software that drives or influences another device takes *that device's* class before Rule 11 is ever reached. `[verified]` A step count synced in from a wearable is probably just display, but it's the question I'd need answered.

## Limits

> This classifies software under MDR Annex VIII implementing rules 3.1–3.7 and Rule 11, retrieved verbatim from EUR-Lex on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover Art. 2(1) qualification, Rules 1–10 or 12–22, Annex XVI, IVDR, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, or national interpretation. Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

Get the qualification determination first — send me the intended purpose as written and I'll run the classification properly. And I'd push back on giving marketing a class at all until that determination exists, since the class on the website is a claim in its own right.

## There probably isn't an MDR class to put on the website

Classification presumes qualification. Annex VIII tells you *which* class a medical device is; it doesn't tell you *whether* something is a medical device. That's Art. 2(1), which is a separate analysis this skill doesn't cover — and on your own description ("no medical claims", logging water/steps/sleep, a wellness score, encouragement messages), it isn't established that you have a device at all.

So the honest position is:

> Before class, the product has to be a medical device under Art. 2(1). Nothing you've given me settles that, and it's a separate analysis. If qualification is already established, tell me and I'll classify. If not, that comes first.

**If it's not a medical device, it has no MDR class.** Not class I — *none*. MDR simply doesn't apply. That's the thing to take back to marketing.

## Why "put the class on the website" is the wrong ask

Two problems worth naming before this becomes copy:

1. **A stated class is itself a regulatory claim.** Publishing "MDR Class I" asserts you're a medical device under MDR — placing a device on the EU market carries registration, technical documentation, a declaration of conformity, CE marking, PMS and vigilance obligations. Claiming a class you haven't conformity-assessed is a worse position than claiming nothing.
2. **Marketing copy feeds back into qualification.** Intended purpose under implementing rule 3.1 is what *you state*, and regulators read your website as evidence of it. "No medical claims" in engineering is undone the moment the site says "helps manage hydration-related conditions" or "detects poor sleep". The website isn't downstream of qualification — it's an input to it.

The useful answer for marketing is usually: say nothing about MDR, and get the claims wording reviewed so the product stays outside scope.

## What would move this into device territory

If any of these are true or planned, qualification needs a real look:

- The wellness score is presented as indicating, screening for, or ruling out a condition (dehydration, sleep apnoea, a cardiac issue) rather than as a general-wellbeing number
- The encouragement messages become individualised advice tied to a condition or a treatment — "your intake is low for your kidney condition", "adjust your medication timing"
- The app takes data from, or feeds into, another device — under implementing rule 3.3 software that drives or influences a device takes that device's class, so an integration with, say, a CGM or an insulin pump changes the analysis before Rule 11 is ever reached
- Any target-population framing around patients or a diagnosed condition

**If** qualification were established, the Rule 11 path on the purpose as you've described it would land at limb 3 — all other software, class I — since a wellness score isn't information for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions and passive habit logging isn't monitoring physiological processes. But I'm giving you that as a conditional, not a conclusion, because the premise isn't met.

The working directory is empty, so this is based on your description rather than the actual code and marketing copy — worth re-checking against the real in-app text before anything ships.

## The answer marketing doesn't want: there isn't one

As described, your app has **no MDR class**, because it isn't a medical device. Classification only exists *inside* the scope of the regulation. Asking "what class are we?" is like asking what horsepower your bicycle has.

So the thing marketing wants — a class number on the website — is not something you can give them. And you shouldn't want to.

## Why it's out of scope

Under MDR (EU 2017/745) Article 2(1), software is a medical device only if the manufacturer intends it for a specific medical purpose: diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment or alleviation of disease, injury or disability. Logging self-reported water, steps and sleep and returning an aggregate "wellness score" plus encouragement isn't any of those.

Recital 19 makes it explicit: software intended for **lifestyle and well-being purposes** is not a medical device. That's your app, near-textbook.

MDCG 2019-11 (the qualification/classification guidance for software) gets you to the same place. You do perform an action on data beyond storage and retrieval — you compute a score — so you pass that step. But you fail the decisive one: the output isn't for the benefit of an individual patient in a medical sense. Generic wellbeing feedback isn't medical information.

## The trap in the request itself

Intended purpose under MDR is established by the manufacturer's labelling, instructions for use, **and promotional and sales materials**. Your website *is* a source of regulatory truth.

So publishing "we're Class I" would be marketing asserting a medical intended purpose you don't have and don't want. Two separate problems:

1. **It's a false claim.** MDR Article 7 prohibits misleading claims, and specifically ascribing to a product functions or properties it doesn't have. Implying medical device status — or CE marking under MDR — when you have neither is exactly what that provision targets.
2. **The number would be wrong anyway.** People assume a low-risk wellness app maps to Class I. Under Rule 11, software that provides information used for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions is **Class IIa** at minimum, and software monitoring physiological processes is IIa (IIb if variations could cause immediate danger). Class I is the residual "all other software" bucket, and post-MDR very little software with a genuine medical purpose lands there. If you were in scope, you'd most likely be looking at IIa — notified body, QMS under ISO 13485, clinical evaluation, post-market surveillance. Not a website badge.

Claiming Class I is the worst of both: legally a misrepresentation, and technically the wrong guess.

## What marketing can actually put on the site

Give them the accurate positive statement instead of a class:

> This app is a lifestyle and wellbeing product. It is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. It does not provide medical advice.

That's a real, quotable, defensible line. If they want something that sounds substantive, the honest version is that you've assessed the app against MDR and determined it's out of scope as a wellbeing product — which is a stronger story than a misapplied class number.

## What would flip you into scope

Worth circulating to whoever writes copy, because this is where these things go wrong — usually in marketing, not engineering:

- Prevention framing: "prevents dehydration", "reduces your risk of X"
- Detection framing: "detects poor sleep", "identifies sleep disorders", "spot early signs of"
- Targeting a condition or patient group: diabetes, hypertension, insomnia, pregnancy
- Presenting the score as a health risk indicator, especially with "consult your doctor if your score drops below…"
- Adding measured physiological parameters (heart rate, SpO2, blood glucose) rather than self-logged behaviour
- Personalised recommendations that read as therapeutic instruction rather than encouragement

The encouragement messages are your softest spot. "Nice work, keep it up" is fine. "Your hydration is low, this can cause headaches — drink more" starts drifting toward alleviation of a symptom.

## What I'd actually do

Write a short qualification rationale and keep it in the repo: a one-paragraph intended purpose statement, your walk through the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps, the conclusion, the date, and who signed off. Re-review it whenever the feature set or the marketing copy changes materially.

That document is what protects you if a regulator ever asks — far more than any class number on a webpage. It also gives marketing a definitive source so they stop improvising.

One caveat: I'm reasoning from the regulation and guidance, not giving you regulatory advice, and I haven't seen your actual claims. If you're going to market in the EU at scale, a regulatory consultant reviewing the finished copy is cheap next to a Rule 11 misclassification. Happy to draft the qualification rationale document if you want a starting point.

Heads-up: web search was blocked in this session, so this is from knowledge as of my May 2026 cutoff rather than verified against the newest MDCG revisions. The core reasoning below is stable, but have someone confirm current guidance text before anything goes live.

## The short answer: you don't have one

MDR classes (I, IIa, IIb, III) only exist for products that *are* medical devices. Classification is step two. Step one is **qualification** — is this a device at all under Article 2(1)?

From your description — logging water/steps/sleep, a weekly score, encouragement messages, no medical claims — this is general wellness/lifestyle software and falls outside MDR scope. There's no diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment or alleviation of disease. So the honest answer for marketing is "not a medical device," not "Class I."

## Why "just say Class I" is the worst possible outcome

I suspect that's where marketing is heading, since it sounds reassuring and low-stakes. It isn't. Class I is not a light-touch label — it means you *are* a medical device manufacturer, which pulls in technical documentation, a QMS (ISO 13485 in practice), clinical evaluation, CE marking, UDI, EUDAMED registration, post-market surveillance and vigilance, a Person Responsible for Regulatory Compliance under Art. 15, and an EU authorised rep if you're established outside the EU.

Affixing a CE mark or claiming device status without having done the conformity assessment is a regulatory offence, not a marketing flourish. And Article 7 separately prohibits claims that mislead users about intended purpose, safety or performance — in either direction.

## The real risk: marketing copy *creates* the intended purpose

Under Art. 2(12), intended purpose is what the manufacturer states in labelling, the instructions for use, **and promotional material**. Your internal position that you make no medical claims is not what a competent authority reads — they read the website. So the page marketing is building is itself the thing that could qualify you as a device.

Lines that would flip you in:

- Framing the score as health status — "your wellness score indicates elevated risk of…"
- Abnormality flagging — "your sleep is unusually low, you may want to see a doctor"
- Naming a condition or population — diabetes, hypertension, insomnia, pregnancy
- Recommendations framed as managing or improving a condition rather than a habit
- Any accuracy claim benchmarked against a clinical measurement

## If you did flip in, it's probably not Class I

Worth knowing so nobody treats the boundary as low-consequence. Rule 11 of Annex VIII sends software that provides information used for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions to **Class IIa**, escalating to IIb or III with the severity of harm; software monitoring physiological processes is also IIa, or IIb for vital parameters where variation could cause immediate danger. In practice Rule 11 pushes nearly all qualifying standalone software to IIa or above — which means a Notified Body, timelines in quarters, and real cost. There is no comfortable Class I landing zone here. You're either out of scope or you're in a genuine certification project.

## What to actually put on the website

A negative statement rather than a class:

> [App] is a general wellness and lifestyle app. It is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, prevent or monitor any disease or medical condition. It does not replace professional medical advice.

Two things I'd pair with that:

1. **Write down the qualification rationale.** A one-to-two page memo walking the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps and concluding "not a device," with the date and the product description it was based on. That memo is what you hand a competent authority if they ever ask, and it's cheap to produce now and expensive to reconstruct later.
2. **Route marketing copy through whoever owns that memo.** The determination is only as good as the claims that stay consistent with it.

Also on marketing's radar even though you're out of MDR scope: consumer-protection rules on health claims, and GDPR — sleep data plus an inferred "wellness score" is plausibly Article 9 health data regardless of your device status.

I'm not a regulatory consultant and this isn't regulatory advice. Given that the entire determination hangs on wording that marketing is about to publish, this is worth an hour of a regulatory affairs professional's time before launch.

graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

As you've described it, there isn't an MDR class — because the app most likely isn't a medical device at all. "Not a device" and "Class I" are different answers, and marketing needs the first one, not the second.

## Why it falls outside MDR

Under Article 2(1) of MDR 2017/745, something is a device only if its **intended purpose** is diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment or alleviation of disease or injury. Recital 19 and MDCG 2019-11 are explicit that software for lifestyle and wellbeing purposes is out of scope, even when it handles health-adjacent data. Logging water, steps and sleep and returning a composite score plus motivational nudges is lifestyle territory as long as nothing in the product frames it against a disease or condition.

Worth knowing: for standalone software the realistic outcomes are basically binary. If you're in scope, Rule 11 pulls almost all standalone software to **Class IIa** or above — notified body, QMS to ISO 13485, clinical evaluation, technical documentation, post-market surveillance. Class I is a rounding error for software under MDR. So the gap between "out of scope" and "in scope" is not a small upgrade.

## What marketing should and shouldn't publish

Do not put a class on the website. Saying "Class I under MDR" asserts you're a regulated device, which is both untrue and self-inflicted: it drags you into obligations you haven't met. Same for a CE mark under MDR, or phrases like "MDR compliant," "MDR certified," or "medically approved" — affixing a CE mark to a non-device is itself a violation.

If they need something to say, the accurate line is along the lines of: *"This app is a general wellness and lifestyle product. It is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease."* That disclaimer is worth having in the app and the store listing too, not just the site.

## The tripwire, which is specifically marketing's problem

Intended purpose under MDR is determined by your labelling, instructions for use **and promotional material**. Marketing copy is the single most common way a wellness app becomes a regulated device. Things that would flip you in scope:

- Framing the wellness score as a health-risk indicator, or as detecting dehydration, sleep disorders, burnout, etc.
- Any prediction or prognosis language — MDR added "prediction and prognosis" to the definition, so "your score suggests you may be at risk of…" is enough.
- Encouragement messages that become individualised advice aimed at managing a condition rather than generic motivation.
- Named conditions in testimonials, SEO copy, or app store keywords (diabetes, insomnia, hypertension).

Given that, I'd suggest marketing route health-adjacent claims past whoever owns regulatory before publishing, rather than after.

## Other regimes that still apply

Being outside MDR doesn't mean unregulated. GDPR is the big one — sleep and activity data may qualify as health data under Article 9 depending on what you infer from it. Unfair commercial practices rules apply to any wellness claim you can't substantiate. If you ship to the UK, the MHRA analysis mirrors this but is a separate determination; in the US, the FDA general wellness guidance would most likely put you under enforcement discretion on these facts.

One caveat: I'm giving you the regulatory logic, not legal advice, and the conclusion depends on copy I haven't seen. Standard practice is to write a short borderline-assessment memo — intended purpose statement, the Article 2(1) analysis, why Rule 11 isn't engaged — signed off and kept on file. It costs an afternoon and is what you'd show a competent authority if anyone ever asks. Happy to draft one if you paste in the current site and app store copy.
